Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, has described his meeting with the Director-General of South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation, Zane Dangor, as cordial and constructive, following the diplomatic row over the presentation of his letters of credence. Fani-Kayode disclosed this in a post on his X handle on Tuesday, saying the meeting addressed mutual concerns about bilateral relations and events over the weekend. “Honoured to have had an excellent meeting with the DG of South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation, Mr Zane Dangor, this morning. “Mutual concerns regarding our bilateral relations and the events over the weekend were discussed,” he wrote. He said both countries looked forward to building on the outcome of the meeting and strengthening their longstanding relations based on mutual respect, friendship and cooperation. “The meeting was cordial and constructive and I look forward to working closely with DIRCO in our collective attempt to further strengthen the ties between our two great nations,” he added. The meeting came after the South African Broadcasting Corporation reported that the country had demarched Fani-Kayode over the controversy surrounding his presentation of diplomatic credentials to President Cyril Ramaphosa and his subsequent remarks on social media. The SABC reported the development on Tuesday, citing a statement by the South African Department of International Relations and Cooperation. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources According to the statement, Dangor met Fani-Kayode to convey South Africa’s concerns over events following the presentation of the Nigerian envoy’s letters of credence and his subsequent comments on social media. “During the meeting, the Director-General conveyed South Africa’s concern regarding events that transpired following the presentation of the High Commissioner’s Letters of Credence to His Excellency President Cyril Ramaphosa, as well as subsequent remarks made on social media,” the statement read. Dangor also drew Fani-Kayode’s attention to Article 41 of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which requires diplomatic agents to conduct official business with the receiving country through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs. “In this regard, it was emphasised that all official communication should be conducted through established diplomatic channels, including DIRCO,” the statement added. South Africa reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening its strategic partnership with Nigeria and maintaining constructive diplomatic engagement based on African solidarity and mutual respect. The diplomatic row followed a controversy that erupted after Fani-Kayode presented his letters of credence to Ramaphosa at the Presidential Guest House in Pretoria on Friday, alongside ambassadors from 14 other countries. The former Minister of Aviation had alleged that the South African Presidency deliberately excluded his introduction and speech from the livestream of the ceremony, while the addresses of other diplomats were broadcast. In a post on his X handle after the event, Fani-Kayode said, “Every single one of the 15 Ambassadors that were present were introduced formally and gave a speech. Curiously, the South African Presidency refused to air the introduction of my goodself and the Nigerian delegation or to air my speech. “They went a step further by cutting us out of the livestream completely and went back on livestream only after my speech was concluded.” He also claimed that he raised the matter with Ramaphosa during a photo session after the ceremony, adding that the South African President directed relevant officials to address his complaint. Fani-Kayode subsequently declined an interview request from the South African Broadcasting Corporation, saying he was dissatisfied with the treatment of the Nigerian delegation. However, Ramaphosa’s spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya, disputed the envoy’s account, saying the President did not intervene in the operations of the public broadcaster. Magwenya said Ramaphosa had merely referred Fani-Kayode to Sophie Mokoena, the SABC’s acting political and foreign editor, as the appropriate person to address his complaint. He described Fani-Kayode’s handling of the complaint as “grossly inappropriate”, arguing that the envoy had misunderstood what he called a minor operational issue. The South African Presidency subsequently released a separate video of Fani-Kayode’s speech on its YouTube channel, hours after the envoy protested its omission from the initial livestream. The disagreement also triggered an exchange between the Nigerian High Commission and Magwenya, with the mission defending Fani-Kayode and insisting that Ramaphosa intervened to resolve the matter.
